lessons.title: What is politics?
lessons.explain: The political scientist Harold Lasswell described politics as deciding 'who gets what, when, how'. It covers how groups make decisions, share resources and settle disagreements, from a family to the United Nations.
lessons.think: Which decision made by people you never voted for affected you most this year?

lessons.title: Power, authority and legitimacy
lessons.explain: Power is the ability to make others do something. Authority is power people accept as rightful. The sociologist Max Weber said authority comes from three sources: tradition (like a monarch), charisma (a magnetic leader) or rules and law (an elected office).
lessons.think: Which kind of authority does a Jubilee host have over the room?
lessons.video: Max Weber three types of authority explained

lessons.title: The state and sovereignty
lessons.explain: A state is a government with control over a territory and its people. Weber defined it as the body that holds a monopoly on the legitimate use of force. Sovereignty means no outside power has authority over it, an idea often traced to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
lessons.think: Is the UK one nation, four nations, or both?
lessons.video: what is a state sovereignty explained

lessons.title: Democracy: direct and representative
lessons.explain: In ancient Athens, eligible citizens voted on laws themselves, though women, slaves and foreigners were excluded. Most democracies now are representative: we elect people to decide for us. Referendums, like Brexit in 2016, are moments of direct democracy.
lessons.think: Which questions, if any, should be decided by referendum rather than by MPs?

lessons.title: Left and right
lessons.explain: The terms come from the French National Assembly in 1789, where supporters of the king sat on the right and supporters of revolution on the left. Today 'left' usually means more equality and state action, 'right' more tradition, markets and individual responsibility, though real views rarely fit neatly on one line.
lessons.think: On which issue do your views not match the side you usually lean towards?
lessons.video: left wing vs right wing explained

lessons.title: Rights and the rule of law
lessons.explain: The rule of law means everyone, including the government, is subject to the same laws. In England it is often traced back to Magna Carta in 1215. The UK's Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into British courts.
lessons.think: Should any right be absolute, or can all of them be limited in some situations?

lessons.title: Parliament: Commons and Lords
lessons.explain: The House of Commons has 650 elected MPs, one for each constituency. The House of Lords is mostly appointed, plus some bishops and a few hereditary peers. The Commons has the final say; the Lords revises and delays laws.
lessons.think: Should the House of Lords be elected?

lessons.title: How elections work: first past the post
lessons.explain: In general elections, the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins, even without a majority. This tends to produce strong single-party governments, but parties can win big majorities on a minority of the national vote. Voters rejected a switch to the Alternative Vote in a 2011 referendum.
lessons.think: Is a stable government worth an unequal result?

lessons.title: The Prime Minister and Cabinet
lessons.explain: The Prime Minister is usually the leader of the largest party in the Commons, not directly elected by the country. They choose the Cabinet, senior ministers who run government departments. Cabinet members are expected to publicly support decisions together.
lessons.think: Should the UK directly elect its Prime Minister?
lessons.video: role of UK prime minister and cabinet explained

lessons.title: The monarch and the constitution
lessons.explain: The UK is a constitutional monarchy: the King is head of state but acts on the advice of ministers. Royal assent turns bills into law, and it has not been refused since 1708. The UK has no single written constitution; its rules come from laws, court rulings and conventions.
lessons.think: What, if anything, does the UK gain from having a monarch?

lessons.title: Devolution: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
lessons.explain: Since 1999, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have had their own parliaments or assemblies with power over areas like health and education. Northern Ireland's system grew from the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 and requires power sharing between unionists and nationalists.
lessons.think: Should England have its own parliament too?

lessons.title: How a law is made
lessons.explain: A bill goes through first reading, second reading (a debate on its main idea), committee stage (line-by-line scrutiny), report stage and third reading in each House. Once both Houses agree, it receives royal assent and becomes an Act of Parliament.
lessons.think: Pick a law that affects your work, like data protection. Who pushed for it?
lessons.video: how a bill becomes law UK

lessons.title: The courts and judges
lessons.explain: Judges in the UK are independent of government. Since 2009 the Supreme Court has been the highest court. Through judicial review, courts can rule that the government acted unlawfully, though they cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.
lessons.think: Should unelected judges be able to overrule elected ministers?
lessons.video: UK supreme court judicial review explained

lessons.title: Local councils and mayors
lessons.explain: Councils run services like bins, social care, libraries and planning. Many English regions now have elected mayors, like the Mayor of London, with powers over transport and housing. Much of their money comes from council tax and central government grants.
lessons.think: Which local decision has the biggest impact on your daily life?

lessons.title: The United Nations
lessons.explain: Founded in 1945 after the Second World War, the UN has 193 member states. Its Security Council has five permanent members with a veto: the US, UK, France, Russia and China. Critics say the veto paralyses it when those powers disagree.
lessons.think: Should the five permanent members keep their veto?
lessons.video: how the united nations works explained

lessons.title: The European Union and Brexit
lessons.explain: The EU began as a coal and steel community in the 1950s and grew into a single market of 27 countries. The UK joined in 1973, voted to leave in 2016 by 52% to 48%, and left on 31 January 2020.
lessons.think: What was the strongest argument from the side of the Brexit vote you disagreed with?

lessons.title: NATO
lessons.explain: A military alliance formed in 1949 between North American and European countries. Under Article 5, an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. It has only been used once, after the 11 September 2001 attacks.
lessons.think: Does a defensive alliance make war more or less likely?

lessons.title: The African Union
lessons.explain: Formed in 2002, replacing the Organisation of African Unity founded in 1963, which Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah championed. It has 55 members and its headquarters is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. It works on peace, trade and a continental free trade area.
lessons.think: What would a more united Africa need to look like to work?

lessons.title: The IMF and World Bank
lessons.explain: Both were set up at Bretton Woods in 1944. The IMF lends to countries in financial crisis; the World Bank funds development. Their loans have often come with conditions such as spending cuts, which critics say hurt the poor and supporters say fix broken finances.
lessons.think: Is it fair for lenders to set conditions on how a country runs itself?

lessons.title: The Commonwealth
lessons.explain: A voluntary association of 56 countries, most once part of the British Empire. Some members, like Rwanda, Gabon and Togo, had no British colonial link. King Charles is its head, though most members are republics.
lessons.think: What is the Commonwealth for, now the empire is gone?

lessons.title: The International Criminal Court
lessons.explain: Based in The Hague since 2002, the ICC tries individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The US, China and Russia are not members. Some African governments have accused it of focusing unfairly on Africa.
lessons.think: Can international justice work if the most powerful countries are outside it?

lessons.title: Colonialism and independence
lessons.explain: By 1914 European powers controlled most of Africa and much of Asia. After the Second World War, independence movements spread. Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, in 1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
lessons.think: How does colonial history still shape the countries on your geography cards?

lessons.title: Immigration
lessons.explain: How many people should come to a country, and who decides? This is one of the most argued-over questions in British politics.

sides.for: Supporters of higher immigration point to labour shortages in care and the NHS, an ageing population and the cultural and economic contribution of migrants.
sides.against: Supporters of lower immigration point to pressure on housing and services, wage competition in some sectors and the right of voters to control borders.

lessons.think: Which argument from the side you lean against is hardest to answer?

lessons.title: Free speech and its limits
lessons.explain: Almost everyone supports free speech in principle. The argument is over where the limits sit: hate speech, misinformation, protest and online abuse.

sides.for: Wider limits: words can cause real harm, especially to minorities, and platforms have a duty to protect users.
sides.against: Fewer limits: who decides what is harmful? Rules can be used to silence unpopular but legitimate views.

lessons.think: Where would you draw the line, and who should enforce it?

lessons.title: Climate policy: how fast?
lessons.explain: Most governments agree emissions must fall. The fight is over speed and cost: who pays, and how quickly to change energy, transport and housing.

sides.for: Faster action: delay makes damage and costs far worse, and green industries create jobs.
sides.against: Slower action: rushed targets push up bills for people who can least afford them, while big emitters abroad carry on.

lessons.think: How would you design a climate policy that poorer households would support?

lessons.title: The welfare state: how much?
lessons.explain: The UK's welfare state grew from the 1942 Beveridge Report. Today the debate is over how generous benefits should be and what should be expected in return.

sides.for: More support: a safety net prevents poverty, protects health and gives people stability to find work.
sides.against: Less support or more conditions: high spending needs high taxes, and generous benefits can discourage work.

lessons.think: What is the strongest case for the view you disagree with here?

lessons.title: Policing and protest
lessons.explain: How much power should police have to stop protests that cause disruption? Recent UK laws have widened those powers.

sides.for: More powers: people have a right to get to work, hospital or school without being blocked.
sides.against: Fewer powers: protest is how ordinary people are heard, and disruption is often the point.

lessons.think: Name a protest from history that was disruptive and is now seen as right. Does that change your view?

lessons.title: Regulating AI and social media
lessons.explain: Governments are deciding how to control powerful technology. The UK's Online Safety Act and the EU's AI Act are two attempts. This one connects directly to your work in governance and risk.

sides.for: Strong rules: harms to children, privacy and democracy are already real, and companies will not fix them alone.
sides.against: Light rules: heavy regulation slows innovation, favours big firms who can afford compliance and pushes development elsewhere.

lessons.think: Which single rule would make the biggest difference?

lessons.title: Reparations for slavery
lessons.explain: Caribbean countries, through CARICOM, have asked former colonial powers, including Britain, for reparations for slavery. When slavery was abolished in 1833, Britain paid compensation to slave owners, not to enslaved people.

sides.for: Supporters say the wealth built on slavery still shapes inequality today, and an apology without repair is empty.
sides.against: Opponents say people alive today should not pay for wrongs they did not commit, and that it is impossible to calculate fairly.

lessons.think: What would a fair form of repair look like, if not money?

lessons.title: Should 16-year-olds vote?
lessons.explain: In Scotland and Wales, 16 and 17-year-olds can already vote in their own parliament and local elections. The question is whether that should apply to UK general elections too.

sides.for: Yes: they can work, pay tax and join the army, and voting young builds a lifelong habit.
sides.against: No: most adult rights start at 18, and young people may be more easily influenced.

lessons.think: What age did you start caring about politics, and why?
